rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to determine which critical pairs improve with a shallower slope and whether the nearly coeluting late cluster changes order. This diagnostic run will guide subsequent window trimming and temperature optimization.

The shallower gradient worsened one early pair and did little for other critical pairs, so test temperature-dependent selectivity at the original slope. Raising temperature may separate the late cluster while keeping the final peak below 10 minutes.

Combine the favorable high temperature with a shallower gradient to spread the late cluster. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset the added gradient time; the first pair will be monitored for compression.

Test the low-temperature end of the selectivity range, since the high-temperature runs still leave an early triplet and a late pair unresolved. A moderate starting fraction should retain the first pair while limiting the time penalty.

Return to 60 C and lower the starting fraction relative to injection 4 to recover first-pair resolution and test selectivity in the early triplet. This gradient should keep the last peak near, but below, 10 minutes.

The first pair appears to cross between starting fractions 0.10 and 0.15, so test 0.20 rather than lowering the start further. A shallower gradient should improve the late critical pair, with the higher starting fraction helping contain retention time.

Continue toward a higher starting fraction and shallower slope to test whether the early crossing opens up and the late pair approaches baseline resolution. The main risks are compression of the first three peaks and a small time penalty.

Keep the best gradient fixed and test a 10 C temperature decrease to shift the early critical triplet away from its crossing. This isolates temperature selectivity while checking whether the late pair and retention time remain acceptable.

Test a shallower version of injection 3 while preserving its well-separated first pair and favorable early-triplet selectivity. The last peak should be close to 10 minutes, allowing a small time cost if the critical pairs improve enough.

Slightly reduce the slope relative to injection 4 by lowering the endpoint, which remains well above the observed elution window. This should improve the late critical pair while using the remaining time margin below 10 minutes.

Fine-tune the best method to a slightly shallower slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, targeting a last peak just below 10 minutes. The endpoint remains above the estimated final elution fraction, while the critical middle and late pairs should gain resolution.

Explore a faster, low-temperature branch where selectivity crossings may separate the late cluster on the opposite side of the conditions tested so far. The low starting fraction protects early retention, and the steep gradient should keep the run comfortably below 10 minutes.

Test whether a modest temperature decrease improves the balance of separations in the early triplet at starting fraction 0.15. Injection 4 has enough time margin to accommodate this change without an expected time penalty.
Combine the shallower slope of injection 11 with an intermediate temperature to balance the early triplet and restore first-pair resolution. The last peak is expected to remain just below 10 minutes.

Test a cooler, slightly steeper variant of injection 8: cooling should improve the compressed early and middle pairs, while the steeper slope limits the time cost. This explores whether those gains outweigh reduced separation in the late cluster.

Balance the improved early selectivity at 40 C against the better late-cluster separation at 60 C using an intermediate temperature. The slope is chosen to use nearly the full 10-minute retention allowance without a substantial time penalty.

Explore a higher-starting-fraction, low-temperature alternative that may open the early triplet after its selectivity crossing. Cooling should help retain the earliest compounds, while the higher start limits the final retention time.

Refine the low-starting-fraction branch with a slope just steeper than injection 10, targeting the final peak just below 10 minutes. The endpoint remains above the estimated final elution fraction, preserving gradient elution while avoiding the previous small time penalty.

Refine the intermediate-temperature branch between injections 16 and 17, aiming to resolve the first pair in the late cluster without sacrificing too much early-triplet separation. This slope should keep the last peak close to 10 minutes.

Slightly flatten injection 20's gradient to spend its remaining retention-time margin on the unresolved pairs. The predicted last peak is near 10 minutes, and the endpoint remains safely above the final elution fraction.

Test one shallower grid-accessible slope around the best method to establish whether additional critical-pair resolution outweighs a small time penalty. This directly brackets the resolution–time optimum near injection 12.

Test the shallower side of the 0.15-start branch to see whether improved early-triplet and late-pair resolution offsets the expected modest time penalty. This checks an untested local alternative to the current best method.

Test a slightly steeper gradient that ends just before the last peak, using the final hold to alter late selectivity without extending the whole gradient. This checks whether a shorter elution time can preserve enough critical-pair resolution to improve on injection 12.

Use the final injection to test a shallower variant of injection 15, where intermediate temperature balanced the early triplet. This checks whether gains in the remaining critical pairs outweigh the modest expected time penalty; injection 12 remains the best observed method.
